cmimc-2017-geometry-01.title: Angle chase
cmimc-2017-geometry-01.body:
The similarity $\triangle ABD\sim\triangle ACB$ gives $\angle ABD=\angle ACB$. Since $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$, $\angle ABC=2\angle ABD=2\angle ACB$. With $\angle ACB=\theta$: $\theta+2\theta+117^\circ=180^\circ$, so $\theta=21^\circ$ and $\angle ABC=42^\circ$.

**Answer: $42$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-02.title: Similar triangles
cmimc-2017-geometry-02.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA=11$, $c=AB=10$. Since $\angle BAD=\angle BCA$ and $\angle B$ is shared, $\triangle ABD\sim\triangle CBA$, so $BD=\frac{c^2}{a}$. Similarly $CE=\frac{b^2}{a}$. Then
$$DE=a-BD-CE=a-\frac{c^2+b^2}{a}=a-\frac{221}{a}=4,$$
so $a^2-4a-221=0$, i.e. $(a-17)(a+13)=0$ and $a=17$. (Triangle $10,11,17$ is indeed obtuse at $A$.)

**Answer: 17**

cmimc-2017-geometry-03.title: Angle bisector and Pythagoras
cmimc-2017-geometry-03.body:
By the Angle Bisector Theorem, $\frac{DC}{AC}=\frac{DB}{AB}=\frac{DC-DB}{AC-AB}=\frac{24}{36}=\frac23$. So $DC+DB=BC=\frac23(AC+AB)$.

From the right triangles with altitude $AE$: $EC^2-EB^2=AC^2-AB^2$, i.e. $(EC-EB)(EC+EB)=(AC-AB)(AC+AB)$. With $EC+EB=BC=\frac23(AC+AB)$:
$$EC-EB=\frac{36}{2/3}=54.$$

**Answer: 54**

cmimc-2017-geometry-04.title: Normal vector
cmimc-2017-geometry-04.body:
Write $\mathcal P$ as $2x+y+kz=10$ (it contains $\ell$ at $z=0$). Its distance from the center $(0,0,1)$ must be $1$: $\frac{|k-10|}{\sqrt{5+k^2}}=1$, so $(10-k)^2=5+k^2$, $100-20k=5$, $k=\frac{19}{4}$. Then $|n|=\sqrt{5+\frac{361}{16}}=\frac{21}{4}$.

The tangency point is the center plus the unit normal (toward the plane): $(x_0,y_0,z_0)=(0,0,1)+\frac{4}{21}\left(2,1,\tfrac{19}{4}\right)$, which has all coordinates positive. So $z_0=1+\frac{19}{21}=\frac{40}{21}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{40}{21}$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-04.title: Cross-section
cmimc-2017-geometry-04.body:
Let $O$ be the origin, $C=(0,0,1)$, and $P$ the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $\ell$; $OP=\frac{5\cdot10}{\sqrt{125}}=2\sqrt5$. In the vertical plane through $O,P,C$ (perpendicular to $\ell$) the sphere is a unit circle and $OP$, $PT$ are the two tangents from $P$, where $T$ is the tangency point. With $\theta=\angle OPC$: $\sin\theta=\frac1{\sqrt{21}}$, $\cos\theta=\frac{2\sqrt5}{\sqrt{21}}$, so $\sin2\theta=\frac{4\sqrt5}{21}$ and $z_0=PT\sin2\theta=2\sqrt5\cdot\frac{4\sqrt5}{21}=\frac{40}{21}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{40}{21}$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-05.title: Radii of orthogonal circles
cmimc-2017-geometry-05.body:
At a common point $P$ the radii $PB$ and $PC$ are perpendicular to the (perpendicular) tangents, so $PB\perp PC$ and $r_B^2+r_C^2=BC^2$.

By tangency, $AT_B^2=AB^2-r_B^2$ and $AT_C^2=AC^2-r_C^2$. Adding:
$$49+121=AB^2+AC^2-BC^2=2\,AB\cdot AC\cos\angle BAC.$$
Also $[ABC]=\frac12AB\cdot AC\sin\angle BAC=20$, so $AB\cdot AC\sin\angle BAC=40$. Hence
$$\tan\angle BAC=\frac{40}{85}=\frac{8}{17}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{8}{17}$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-06.title: C is the incenter of APQ
cmimc-2017-geometry-06.body:
$\angle BAD=180^\circ-70^\circ-50^\circ=60^\circ$, so $\angle BCD=120^\circ$ (cyclic) and $\angle PCQ=120^\circ$. Since $BC=CD$, $AC$ bisects $\angle BAD$, i.e. $\angle PAQ$. The incenter $I$ of $\triangle APQ$ satisfies $\angle PIQ=90^\circ+\frac{60^\circ}2=120^\circ$, so $P,C,I,Q$ are concyclic; as $A,I,C$ are collinear, $I=C$. Thus $C$ is the incenter of $\triangle APQ$.

Now $\angle BDC=\angle BAC=30^\circ=\angle CBD$ (as $BC=CD$), so $\angle APD=\angle ABD-\angle BDC=70^\circ-30^\circ=40^\circ$ and $\angle AQB=\angle ADB-\angle DBC=50^\circ-30^\circ=20^\circ$. Then
$$\angle APQ-\angle AQP=2(\angle APC-\angle AQC)=2(40^\circ-20^\circ)=40^\circ.$$

**Answer: $40$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-07.title: Reduce to a triangle
cmimc-2017-geometry-07.body:
$\omega$ is the incircle of $\triangle PXY$ and $\Omega$ is its $P$-excircle. So we want side $a=XY$ of a triangle with inradius $r=4$, circumradius $R=9$, and with $XY$ bisecting $PC_\Omega$ (the segment from vertex to the excenter), i.e. the altitude from $P$ equals the exradius $r_a$.

With area $K=\frac12ar_a=r_a(s-a)$ we get $a=2(s-a)$, so $b+c=2a$ and $s=\frac32a$. Then $K=rs=6a$, and $K=\frac{abc}{4R}=\frac{abc}{36}$ gives $bc=216$.

Heron: $K^2=s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$ gives $36a^2=\frac32a\cdot\frac12a\,(s-b)(s-c)$, so $(s-b)(s-c)=48$. Also $(s-b)(s-c)=s^2-s(b+c)+bc=\frac94a^2-3a^2+216=216-\frac34a^2$. So $\frac34a^2=168$, $a^2=224$ and $a=4\sqrt{14}$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt{14}$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-08.title: Radical axis
cmimc-2017-geometry-08.body:
Let $X,Y$ be the projections of $B,C$ on the directrix. By the parabola property $BX=BA$ and $CY=CA$, so the directrix is tangent at $X$ to the circle $\omega_B$ (center $B$, radius $AB$) and tangent at $Y$ to $\omega_C$ (center $C$, radius $AC$). The circles meet at $A$ and its reflection $A'$ across $BC$, so line $AD$ is their radical axis and $T$ (on it and on the common tangent) is the midpoint of $XY$.

Power of the point $T$: $TX^2=TA\cdot TA'=(TD+AD)(TD-AD)=TD^2-AD^2$. And $TX=\frac12XY=\frac12\sqrt{BC^2-(AC-AB)^2}=\frac12\sqrt{400-16}=4\sqrt6$.

So $DT^2-DA^2=96$.

**Answer: 96**

cmimc-2017-geometry-09.title: Radical center and a parallelogram
cmimc-2017-geometry-09.body:
$DE$ is antiparallel to $BC$, so $\triangle ADE\sim\triangle ABC$. Let $P$ be the foot from $A$ to $BC$, which is the concurrency point. $BC$ is the radical axis of $\odot(ABC)$ and $\odot(BOC)$, and $DE$ that of $\odot(BOC)$ and $\odot(ADE)$, so $P$ is the radical center and $AP$ is the radical axis of $\odot(ABC)$ and $\odot(ADE)$; hence $A,D,Q,E$ are concyclic.

Angle chasing gives $\angle ADO=\angle OBC=90^\circ-\angle A$, so $DO\perp AB$ and similarly $EO\perp AC$: $O$ is the orthocenter of $\triangle ADE$. Then $AO$ and $AP$ are isogonal, so $AQ$ is a diameter of $\odot(ADE)$ and $ODQE$ is a parallelogram. Hence
$$2(OD^2+OE^2)=OQ^2+DE^2=OA^2+DE^2=(2R'\cos A)^2+(2R'\sin A)^2=4R'^2=AQ^2,$$
where $R'$ is the circumradius of $\triangle ADE$. So $AQ=\sqrt{2(9+49)}=\sqrt{116}=2\sqrt{29}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{29}$**

cmimc-2017-geometry-10.title: Key angle is 60 degrees
cmimc-2017-geometry-10.body:
Let $O_b,O_c$ and $H_b,H_c$ be the circumcenters and orthocenters of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$. One checks $\triangle AO_bO_c\sim\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DH_bH_c$ (all directly similar, using $\angle AO_bB=\angle AO_cC$ and $DH_b\perp AB$, $DH_c\perp AC$). The Euler lines are $O_bH_b$ and $O_cH_c$; parallel means $H_bO_b\parallel H_cO_c$, which makes the intersection $P$ of $H_bH_c$ and $O_bO_c$ the center of the spiral similarity taking $\triangle DH_bH_c$ to $\triangle AO_bO_c$. Since $O_bO_c$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AD$, $PD=PA$ and the two triangles are congruent, so $DH_b=AO_b=R$, where $R$ is the circumradius of $\triangle ABD$. But in triangle $ABD$ the distance from vertex $D$ to the orthocenter is $2R|\cos\angle ADB|$, so $2R|\cos\angle ADB|=R$ and $\angle ADB=60^\circ$ in the valid configuration (with $D$ on side $BC$).

Let $X$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$: $BX=5$, $CX=9$, $AX=12$. Then $DX=\frac{12}{\tan60^\circ}=4\sqrt3$, with $D$ on the side of $X$ toward $C$, so
$$\frac{BD}{CD}=\frac{5+4\sqrt3}{9-4\sqrt3}=\frac{93+56\sqrt3}{33}.$$
(Numerically $\approx5.757$; confirmed by direct computation with coordinates.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{93+56\sqrt3}{33}$**
